everyday_analogy.title: One tiny everyday analogy
everyday_analogy.setup: If students with tutors score lower on the final exam, that does not prove tutoring is harmful.
everyday_analogy.better_interpretation: The weaker students were more likely to get tutors, so the tutor group started off at a disadvantage.

fictional_examples.title: Illustration 1: treated patients started older and sicker

treated_group.label: Received hormone therapy
treated_group.profile: Older on average, more later-stage disease, more positive lymph nodes

untreated_group.label: Did not receive hormone therapy
untreated_group.profile: Younger on average, more early-stage disease, fewer positive lymph nodes

fictional_examples.wrong_conclusion: Hormone therapy looks harmful because the treated group did worse.
fictional_examples.better_interpretation: The treated group already had worse baseline prognosis, so the crude comparison is unfair.

fictional_examples.title: Illustration 2: the treated group had a riskier subtype mix

treated_group.label: Received hormone therapy
treated_group.profile: More high-risk subtype mix and more advanced baseline features

untreated_group.label: Did not receive hormone therapy
untreated_group.profile: Healthier subtype mix and milder baseline disease

fictional_examples.wrong_conclusion: The therapy must be the reason the treated group looked worse.

real_case.title: The one real completed case study so far

before_text.headline: Before adjustment
before_text.summary: The first crude comparison made hormone therapy look harmful.
before_text.detail: But the treated and untreated groups were not similar at baseline. They differed strongly in stage, nodal burden, age, menopausal state, and subtype mix.

after_text.headline: After overlap weighting
after_text.summary: Measured balance improved sharply and the estimate moved toward about 1.00.
after_text.detail: That tells us the naive comparison was misleading. It does not prove the final treatment effect.

methods.name: Overlap weighting
methods.problem: The treated and untreated groups overlap only partly.
methods.helps: It gives more weight to patients who realistically could have gone either way.
methods.cannot: It still cannot fix important confounders that were never measured.

methods.name: Propensity score matching
methods.problem: A crude comparison mixes together patients who were not similar at baseline.
methods.helps: It tries to pair treated and untreated patients who looked more alike before treatment.
methods.cannot: It can discard unmatched patients and still cannot remove hidden confounding.

ai_connection.problem: Without adjustment, the final AI model may learn a false pattern like 'treatment looks harmful' only because sicker patients received it.
ai_connection.benefit: Adjustment tries to give the model a cleaner treatment signal by reducing unfair baseline differences.
flow: Estimated outcomes under several treatment options
ai_connection.future_work: This is the intended Stage 2 direction of BRCAPath-Rx, not a finished multi-treatment recommendation engine yet.

limitations: This is still observational data, not a randomized trial.
Adjustment helps, but it does not magically prove causality.
Important confounders are still missing, including comorbidity, adherence, exact regimen, and treatment-era detail.
say_aloud: This page uses short examples to show why a raw treated-versus-untreated comparison can mislead us, then shows the one real completed Stage 2 case study. The real point is that the naive result changed a lot after adjustment, which means the crude comparison was not trustworthy.
